SATOM 1.9.3

SATOM speaks your language, change requests become a complete, signable change process for every Forti product, and directory sign-in gains RADIUS import, an approval gate and several sources in order.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-08-10 · All releases

In short#

1.9.3 is a large release with three themes. The whole console can now be shown in Spanish, German, French or Italian, chosen from your profile. Change requests grow into a full change process: a guided form that proposes the wording, a formal change document in several languages, saved pre-flight evidence, maintenance windows on your own clock, NetBox and external approval, and a notice to affected users when the window closes. And sign-in through a directory gains RADIUS user import, an approval gate for new accounts and support for several sign-in sources at once. Operators who raise changes and administrators who manage users will notice the most.

What's new#

The console in your language#

  • The menus, buttons and pages of the console are now translated into Spanish, German, French and Italian, not only English.
  • SATOM picks the language in this order: the language saved in your profile, then your browser's language (if SATOM ships it), then English.
  • Translations are prepared in advance and stored with the product. Pages never wait for an AI model to translate them, the same button always has the same name, and an installation without access to an AI service still shows its menus in your language.
  • A wrong translation can be corrected in the translation files without a new release.

Your language is a profile setting#

  • Profile → Language stores the language you work in against your own account. It is not shared with other users and does not depend on a browser cookie.
  • The user menu in the top bar shows your current choice next to the entry that changes it.
  • "No preference" and "English" are kept apart. If you have no preference, the change request form asks you which language to use and tells you where to set a preference so it stops asking. If you chose English on purpose, it is not asked again.
  • If you pick a language the change document cannot yet be produced in, your choice is kept, and the change request form says so and asks, rather than quietly producing a document in another language.

Change documents in five languages#

  • The formal change document can now be produced in English, German, Spanish, French and Italian.
  • A language is only offered when every sentence the document can print exists for it and is up to date. If even one is missing, the whole language is withdrawn from the picker, so you never get a document that is half in one language and half in another under an approver's signature.

The formal change document#

Every change request can now be viewed or downloaded as a formal change document (Markdown). It has thirteen numbered sections: general information, purpose, affected systems, justification, impact, risk, rollback, prerequisites, work to be performed, post-change validation, communication plan, approvals and outcome.

  • Purpose, impact, risk, work and validation are written specifically for each of the change-controlled actions.
  • A firmware upgrade is described as what it is on a Fortinet appliance (uploading a firmware image and rebooting into it), never as operating-system patching, so the approver signs what will actually happen.
  • A custom API call prints exactly what will be sent and does not guess at its impact.
  • The approvals section prints the one approval SATOM actually records and leaves the other roles blank for a handwritten signature, instead of inventing them.
  • Each change request now has a permanent human reference (for example CR-2026-0042), a change owner and a document language. The reference is set once and never renumbered, even after a restore.

A guided "New Change Request" form#

New Change Request now asks two questions first, in this order:

  1. The document language.
  2. The type of change.

From those two answers, plus the pre-flight run the change cites, SATOM proposes the title, reason, rollback plan, change owner and notification recipients.

  • The language comes first because all proposed text is written in it.
  • The device list and the maintenance window are not proposed: those are decisions for you, and a guessed window is worse than an empty one.
  • The proposed wording describes this change: the action, the devices, and the cited run's number, time, verdict, firmware and configuration backup. A backup that did not complete is never named in a rollback plan.
  • As soon as you type in a field, SATOM stops updating it, so changing an answer later never wipes your words. Restore proposal puts the suggested text back.
  • The change owner (your account) and the recipients (the default recipients from Settings → Email) are filled in visibly in the fields, so you can see who the change is attributed to before you save.
  • The form still works with JavaScript turned off; the two questions are simply shown all at once.

Administrator-owned change types#

A new page, Administration → Change Types, controls the options in the type of change picker and every sentence a type contributes: the proposed title, reason and rollback plan, and the eight paragraphs the printed document quotes (purpose, justification, impact, downtime, risk, rollback steps, work and validation).

  • Built-in types can be reworded. Overrides are per field: correcting one paragraph keeps the product's wording for the others, and future product corrections still reach the fields you did not change. Leaving a box empty keeps the product's wording; it does not blank that section.
  • Types you add are documentary. The change request is raised, approved and printed, and the work itself is done by hand. Whether a type can be run automatically is never a setting; the form tells you before you pick it, and the Schedule button is not offered for it.
  • Saving translates the changed fields into the other four languages automatically. Each translation run is recorded with its time and token count.
  • Machine translations stay labelled as machine translations, with the model's name. Marking one as reviewed records who accepted it. Text you typed yourself in another language is never overwritten, and editing the source marks the translations as stale instead of deleting them.
  • Approval freezes the wording. When a change request is approved, its text is captured in every document language, and the document prints that copy. Correcting a paragraph later does not rewrite documents already signed. Drafts always show the current wording.
  • Hiding a built-in type removes it from the form only; the action itself stays in the product. Deleting a type you created leaves the change requests already raised with it fully printable.
  • The page is reachable from the Administration group of every ADOM.

Change requests for every Forti product#

  • Change requests are no longer limited to FortiWeb. FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator appliances can now be named in a change window, and the page is reachable from every ADOM.
  • Each ADOM shows only the change requests for its own devices, including when you open one directly by its link.
  • More actions are now under change control: enabling and disabling policies and back-end servers, changing back-end configuration, swapping certificates, the certificate lifecycle sweep and custom API calls join the firmware upgrade. The list is now built automatically from the actions marked as dangerous, so a future dangerous action arrives already gated.
  • A new Reboot action reboots an appliance inside an approved window. It is only offered for products where the reboot call has been verified on real hardware; other products are refused by name.

The Automation section in every ADOM#

Scheduled Actions, Device Provisioning and Change Requests now appear in the Global, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator consoles, and in any ADOM added later.

  • Each ADOM shows only its own scheduled actions, also when you edit, toggle, delete, run or view the history of one directly.
  • The scheduled-action editor offers only the actions that apply to this ADOM, and its device picker lists the devices of this ADOM (it used to be empty outside FortiWeb).
  • System Provisioning stays FortiWeb-only on purpose: its profiles are made of FortiWeb configuration objects that other products do not have.

Upgrade preparation leads to a change request#

  • Each pre-flight ("Upgrade preparation") run is now saved. Every stored run is listed on the page with its verdict, and a finished run offers Raise change request with the appliance, the action and the run already filled in.
  • Saved runs cannot be changed afterwards, so the run an approved change cites is exactly the run that was taken.
  • The verdict only grades the checks you asked for. A published service that was already unreachable before the change is recorded as the baseline, not as a failure.
  • View result on every row of the runs table opens the full saved run: the health checks, the backup filename and the per-policy baseline. It is shown exactly like a live run, but clearly labelled as recorded, with its run number, time and who ran it.
  • The list of published services a window takes offline is now shown with each run, not only as a count. Each service is shown as reachable, unreachable or not probed; "not probed" is never shown as either up or down.

The affected services are frozen onto the change#

  • When a change request is raised, the list of affected services is captured and stored with it. The detail page, the document and the export all use that snapshot, so the document that was approved and the record of what ran are the same.
  • You can ask to compare the snapshot with the devices as they are now. Any difference is reported, never merged in silently.
  • Export the inventory as Excel (.xlsx) or CSV with the columns you choose. Columns always appear in the same order, and choosing none exports the five default columns. The column names match what you see on screen.

Change requests on your local clock#

  • Window start and end are now read in the timezone set under Settings → General, and the window fields name that timezone. Before, times were shown in local time but saved as if typed in UTC, so a window entered as 22:00 could open hours later than announced.
  • Daily, weekly and monthly scheduled actions now also run at the local time you set. "Every night at 02:00" means 02:00 local time, all year round.
  • Scheduling a firmware upgrade from the appliance page also uses the configured timezone.

NetBox maintenance windows#

Settings → Integrations can now connect SATOM to NetBox (address, an encrypted token, TLS verification, a timeout and a mapping of appliances to NetBox devices).

  • When a change request starts running, SATOM opens a maintenance window in NetBox, and closes it with the outcome when the run ends.
  • It works with any NetBox, with or without plugins. You choose how the window is recorded: a journal entry, a device tag, or device custom fields.
  • Window times are always sent with an explicit timezone, so NetBox cannot shift them by hours.

Integration hooks#

You can now add small Python scripts that SATOM runs when something happens: a change is requested or approved, a window opens or closes, or an upgrade finishes or fails. For example, a hook can open a ticket in your own system and hand the ticket reference back to the change request.

  • Hooks never run inside the web console. A separate, restricted runner executes them with a time limit and only the secrets the hook declares.
  • A script with a syntax error is refused when you save it, with the error message, instead of failing during a maintenance window.
  • Output is shortened and any declared secret is hidden before it is stored.

External approval that fails closed#

  • A change request can be bound to an external change authority (Approval → External). It then only runs once that authority has explicitly approved it. No answer, a slow answer, an unclear answer or never having asked all count as "not approved".
  • Withdrawing an approval clears it, so it can no longer open a window.
  • Existing change requests default to Manual approval and behave as before.
  • The change request page shows the external ticket reference and link, the state of the window in NetBox and an integration log. "None requested" and "error" are shown as different states.

Affected users are told when the window closes#

  • When a window closes, success or failure, SATOM emails the people on the change request's Notify on completion list, with the reason. If that list is empty it uses the default recipients from Settings → Email; if neither is set, nothing is sent and the change request records why.
  • The notice is sent once and is separate from the warning sent before the window.
  • If the email cannot be sent, the change keeps its real outcome and the notice can be retried.

Directory sign-in: RADIUS import, approval gate, several sources#

  • Import users from FortiAuthenticator / RADIUS. Settings → Authentication → Sync directory users now works for RADIUS too, not only AD/LDAP. Because RADIUS cannot list users, SATOM reads the group members from a FortiAuthenticator already registered under Appliances, using its existing API key. Sign-in itself still goes over RADIUS. Pick the appliance and the group in the RADIUS section.
  • Several import groups, each with its own profile. For example, one group can be imported as operators and another as read-only users in a single run. A user in two groups gets the profile of the first row; a blank profile uses the global default.
  • A group name the appliance does not have stops the whole import and lists the groups that do exist, so a typo cannot silently import nobody or a partial roster.
  • Approval gate for directory users (Settings → Authentication, for every external source). When it is on, someone signing in from the directory for the first time gets a disabled account and sees awaiting administrator approval until an administrator enables it and gives it a profile under Users. Existing accounts are not affected.
  • Several sign-in sources, in order. You can now enable Active Directory, LDAP and RADIUS together, in an order you choose; the first source that accepts the user wins. The local database is always available as a fallback so nobody is locked out. The page explains why order matters: an unreachable source waits for its full timeout before the next one is tried, and a wrong password counts against the lockout policy of every source tried before the right one.

What changes for you#

  • New directory accounts start as read-only, not operator. Giving more rights is an explicit administrator action. An unknown profile name always falls back to fewer rights, never more.
  • A live firmware upgrade now needs an approved, open change window. This applies to the upgrade button on the appliance page as well as to scheduled upgrades. Dry runs are not gated, because they send nothing to the appliance. An authorised upgrade moves its change request to in progress and closes it with the real outcome.
  • The per-username allowlist is removed (Settings → Access Control → Allowed Users). Profiles decide what a user may do, and the directory group decides who may sign in. If your installation had a list stored, you are told at startup and on the Access Control page, with a button to clear it. The IP whitelist on the same card stays.
  • New Change Request no longer pre-selects a type. The type picker starts on a "Choose the type of change" prompt, so choosing any type always takes effect. Arriving from an appliance's pre-flight page still fills it in.
  • Upgrade preparation is now also offered for FortiADC.
  • The certificate lifecycle sweep is now marked as dangerous. It deletes certificate material from the appliance, so the console now warns before it runs and it can be put under change control.
  • "Clients affected by this window" now reads FortiADC virtual servers as well as FortiWeb server policies; before, every FortiADC looked like it had no clients.
  • Settings → Default appliance platform now lists all four product families (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer) and no longer offers "FortiWeb-Cloud", which SATOM cannot manage. Registering a new appliance now actually starts on that platform, as the help text always said. Values saved before still read back correctly.
  • One SATOM logo everywhere. The console, the project site and the product site now show the same SATOM emblem and icons.
  • The appearance preset named "Fortinet" has been removed from the settings; the similar "Ember Red" remains. No installation's look changes.
  • The installation manual is now in English. Section numbers, commands and paths are unchanged.

Fixed#

  • Deleting an object that others still use is refused. SATOM now checks the appliance's own reference count before deleting and, when it can, names the objects that still point at it. The check also runs on Preview, so the refusal appears before the confirmation prompt. An object whose references cannot be read is not deleted; an administrator can force the delete when the firmware's count is wrong, and the audit log records that it was forced.
  • A change request could never finish. After its action ran, it stayed at scheduled forever. It now moves to in progress and then to completed or failed. A run that was skipped counts as failed, with the reason shown.
  • Upgrade preparation could run without approval. The maintenance-window gate only applied to the firmware upgrade itself; every action bound to a change request is now gated.
  • The new change request form accepted invalid choices. An unknown action was silently turned into an upgrade; it is now rejected. Devices of a product the action does not support, or several devices for a single-device action, are refused when you save instead of failing at window time.
  • Choosing the first change type did nothing. Picking the entry that was already selected never showed the next step or the proposed wording.
  • The login page itself could be blocked. Simply viewing it five times in a minute (after a logout and a couple of reloads) showed "Too Many Requests" without any password having been tried. The limit now only counts actual sign-in attempts, and the page stays readable while attempts are throttled.
  • Signing in could sign you straight back out when you had arrived at the login page from the logout link.
  • FortiAuthenticator appliances could show as offline while they were answering normally.
  • Device output was nearly invisible. The grey panels used for SSH health checks, the inspector, the git consoles in Settings and the change document had very low contrast. They are now readable, keep CLI columns aligned and scroll instead of stretching the page.
  • Upgrade preparation results overflowed their tiles when a firmware build or backup filename was long. The backup filename now has its own line.
  • The Upgrade preparation page looked different from the rest of the console, and a policy name containing < could hide the rest of its row.
  • Translation never produced any text. Every translation request came back empty and was reported as the AI provider's fault. It now works.
  • Translations could damage the document. Placeholders such as device names or field names were sometimes translated too; a translation that changes them is now retried once and then refused.
  • Stray markers from the translator could appear in the interface (for example in the navigation under AI Advisor). They are now removed and caught.
  • A page could crash if a translated string contained a stray percent sign.
  • A corrected translation could keep showing the old text. A check now catches translation files that were fixed but not rebuilt.
  • The About card in your profile said "v1.0". It now shows the real version, and described SATOM as a FortiWeb-only console; it now describes the product correctly and is translated.

Before you upgrade#

  • Firmware upgrades started by hand now need an approved change request with an open window. Plan to raise and approve one before your next live upgrade.
  • New directory users default to read-only. If you relied on new directory users getting operator rights, set a profile per import group or adjust each user under Users.
  • The per-username allowlist no longer applies. Review who can sign in through your directory groups and, if prompted on the Access Control page, clear the old list.
  • Consider turning on the approval gate for directory users if you allow sign-in from several sources.

Under the hood#

  • Integration hooks run in a separate, locked-down service, never inside the web console. A setup problem that made queued hooks silently never run was fixed before release.
  • The Excel export is built into SATOM, so offline installations need no extra software.
  • The vendor's logo file is no longer served from SATOM; only the product-type icons that label each appliance remain.
  • A software dependency needed for translations is now part of the standard install, so a reinstall cannot remove it.
